source.title_on_document: The Pedagogical Impact of ChatGPT on High-school Student’s Creative Writing Skills: An Exploration of Generative AI Assisted Writing Tools

paper_design_summary: The paper reports random allocation of 84 eleventh-grade students at a Thai secondary school to ChatGPT-integrated writing lessons or conventional Communicative Language Teaching, although it labels the design quasi-experimental (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 20-21). Both groups received 20 hours of lessons, and the researcher and two native speakers scored narratives written without electronic devices or internet access before and after instruction (PDF pp. 5-10, printed pp. 21-26). Results compare the total creative-writing rubric score between groups at posttest and within the ChatGPT group from pretest to posttest (PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 27-28, Tables 3-4).

studies.label: ChatGPT-integrated creative-writing lessons and unassisted writing posttest

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were allocated to Group A, receiving ChatGPT-integrated lessons, or Group B, receiving conventional lessons. The document separately states random sampling of the school sample and random allocation to the two groups. Coded as a field RCT because allocation is explicitly described as random and the intervention occurred in school writing lessons; the authors’ quasi-experimental label is retained as a reporting inconsistency.
assignment.quote: Employing a simple random sampling method, these students were then allocated into two distinct groups, namely Group A (Experimental Group) and Group B (Controlled Group), each comprising 42 students.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 21), Population and Samples; corroborating random group-allocation statement and quasi-experimental label in PDF p. 4 (printed p. 20), Methodology; classroom lesson setting in PDF pp. 5-6 (printed pp. 21-22), Research Instruments.

arms.name: Group A (Experimental Group)
arms.description: Communicative Language Teaching integrated with ChatGPT for outlining, drafting, revisions, and feedback; 10 lesson plans for 20 hours (PDF pp. 5-6, printed pp. 21-22, Research Instruments, item 1). Allocation N = 42 is stated in Population and Samples (PDF p. 5); analyzed N = 42 is explicitly printed for the pretest in Table 2 (PDF p. 10). The posttest N is not separately printed in Tables 3-4.

arms.name: Group B (Controlled Group)
arms.description: Conventional Communicative Language Teaching without AI-assisted writing tools, with the same teaching stages and 10 lesson plans for 20 hours (PDF p. 6, printed p. 22, Research Instruments, item 2). Allocation N = 42 is stated in Population and Samples (PDF p. 5); analyzed N = 42 is explicitly printed for the pretest in Table 2 (PDF p. 10). The posttest N is not separately printed in Table 4.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are stated. The analyzed count records the documented study sample and the explicit pretest analysis counts of 42 students per arm in Table 2; it is not an independently reported posttest count. Tables 3-4 give no final analyzed N or number of complete pre/post pairs, so posttest retention cannot be confirmed. The paper is not described here as an intention-to-treat analysis.
participants.who: Eleventh-grade students at Angsilapittayakom School, sampled during the second semester of the 2023 academic year from the Thai secondary-school setting (PDF p. 5, printed p. 21, Population and Samples).
participants.quote: A meticulous multi-stage sampling method was employed to randomly select 84 eleventh- grade students from Angsilapittayakom School as the study’s samples.
participants.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 21), Population and Samples: sample of 84 and allocation of 42 per group; PDF p. 10 (printed p. 26), Table 2: analyzed pretest N = 42 per group; PDF p. 1 (printed p. 17), Abstract: Thai school context. Posttest Tables 3-4 are PDF pp. 11-12 (printed pp. 27-28).

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, paid version; specific language model and model version not stated (PDF p. 6, printed p. 22, Research Instruments).
ai_tool.how_used: Students were granted access to ChatGPT during their lessons to generate outlines, draft, refine ideas, revise content, and obtain feedback. Introductory training covered the interface, generating prompts, interpreting suggestions, and incorporating feedback. This is coded as open_chat because students directly used the tool, with both ideation and refinement functions (PDF pp. 5-6, printed pp. 21-22, Research Instruments, item 1). ChatGPT was unavailable during the scored pretest and posttest because devices and internet resources were prohibited (PDF pp. 7, 9-10, printed pp. 23, 25-26).

task.description: Students selected a researcher-provided prompt and wrote a narrative; the posttest used a different prompt from the pretest. Example prompts concerned an abandoned house, a deserted island, a journal entry, and a dialogue in a mysterious situation. Narratives typically ranged from 300 to 500 words (PDF pp. 7-8, printed pp. 23-24, Research Instruments, item 3; PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Data Collection, step 4).
task.duration: 10 lesson plans covering 20 hours in each group; 50 minutes for each pretest and posttest narrative. The calendar span of instruction and any interval in days after the last lesson are not stated (PDF pp. 5-7, 9-10, printed pp. 21-23, 25-26).

outcomes.name: Creative writing skills total score at the unassisted posttest
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Total score of 25 points across five dimensions worth 5 points each: Creativity, Development, Voice, Literary Devices, and Literary Conventions (PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp. 24-25, Table 1; PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 27-28, Tables 3-4). The researcher and two native speakers rated each student’s narrative; their method of combining ratings and blinding are not stated (PDF p. 7, printed p. 23, Research Instruments, item 3). The three experts who validated the rubric are not identified as the same people as these raters. The total combines creative and writing-quality criteria. The five components are inventoried below, but no component-specific results are reported. The main analysis compares students’ posttest scores between groups; the paired pre/post analysis uses the same outcome (PDF p. 11, printed p. 27, Data Analysis). Devices and internet resources were prohibited during both assessments, explicitly including the posttest (PDF pp. 7, 9-10, printed pp. 23, 25-26).
outcomes.delay: No interval in days is stated; the posttest was conducted upon completion of the teaching sessions (PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Data Collection, step 4).

contrasts.reported: Posttest total score (25 points): Group A M = 22.72, S.D. = 5.72; Group B M = 19.82, S.D. = 7.42; t = 14.46; Sig. = 0.00*. The table footnote states significance at a 0.01 level. These are the printed values. Table 4 does not give posttest N, degrees of freedom, standard errors, confidence intervals, or standardized effects. The available arm Ns are Group A N = 42 and Group B N = 42 in the pretest Table 2; these are not independently confirmed posttest Ns.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 12 (printed p. 28), Table 4 and accompanying Findings text; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 27), Data Analysis, item 3; arm Ns only in PDF p. 10 (printed p. 26), Table 2.

contrasts.reported: Group A total score (25 points): before the integration of Generative AI tools M = 11.46, S.D. = 7.12; after the integration of Generative AI tools M = 22.72, S.D. = 5.72; paired-samples t = 17.91; Sig. = 0.00*. The table footnote states significance at a 0.01 level. Table 3 does not give the number of complete pairs, degrees of freedom, standard errors, confidence intervals, or standardized effects. Group A N = 42 is printed in the pretest Table 2. This is a within-group change, not an independent randomized contrast.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 27), Table 3, Findings, and Data Analysis, item 2; pretest N in PDF p. 10 (printed p. 26), Table 2.

The empty contrasts array means no separate result is available, not evidence of no difference. Electronic devices and internet resources were prohibited at the posttest (PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Data Collection, step 4).

company_involvement.description: No company involvement is stated. The sole author’s listed affiliation is Angsilapittayakom School; the paper describes use of paid ChatGPT but does not report company funding, authorship, or support.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 17), author affiliation; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 22), paid-version description; no funding or conflict-of-interest statement appears in the PDF.

eligibility.reason: The methods explicitly state random allocation of students to AI-integrated versus conventional lessons, despite the quasi-experimental label (PDF pp. 4-5, printed pp. 20-21). The study sample is 84 people, with analyzed pretest N = 42 per arm in Table 2 (PDF pp. 5 and 10, printed pp. 21 and 26); posttest Ns are not separately given and retention remains an audit question. Creativity is scored on student-produced narratives through a rubric that includes inventiveness and originality (PDF pp. 7-9, printed pp. 23-25, assessment description and Table 1), with total-score results in Tables 3-4 (PDF pp. 11-12, printed pp. 27-28). The eligible question is after_ai: the posttest explicitly prohibited electronic devices and internet resources (PDF p. 10, printed p. 26, Data Collection, step 4).

one_line_finding: On the unassisted posttest, the ChatGPT-lesson group scored M = 22.72 (S.D. = 5.72) versus M = 19.82 (S.D. = 7.42) for conventional lessons on the 25-point total; Table 4 prints t = 14.46 and Sig. = 0.00* (PDF p. 12, printed p. 28).
open_questions: Confirm how random group allocation was implemented: PDF pp. 4-5 (printed pp. 20-21) explicitly describe it as random but also label the design quasi-experimental; no allocation algorithm or concealment details are given.

Confirm final posttest sample sizes and the number of complete pre/post pairs. Table 2 explicitly gives 42 students per arm at pretest, whereas Tables 3-4 omit Ns and no attrition account is given (PDF pp. 10-12, printed pp. 26-28).

Audit the printed test statistics against the underlying data, especially Table 4’s t = 14.46 and Sig. = 0.00* alongside the reported group means and SDs. These are transcribed without correction; no effect sizes or replacement test statistics have been calculated (PDF p. 12, printed p. 28).

The paper does not explain how the researcher’s and two native speakers’ ratings were combined, whether raters were blinded, or provide separate results for the rubric components (PDF pp. 7-9 and 11-12, printed pp. 23-25 and 27-28).
notes: All locators give the PDF page first and the printed journal page second; printed pagination runs from 17 to 34. Read all 18 PDF pages and all 411 markdown lines, including the references; no appendix or supplementary material is mentioned. Outcome inventory: Figures 1-2 show teaching procedures only (PDF pp. 6-7); Table 1 defines five scored rubric components (PDF pp. 8-9); Table 2 reports the baseline total (PDF p. 10); Tables 3-4 report the same total for the paired pre/post and between-group posttest comparisons (PDF pp. 11-12). Six outcome entries comprise one reported total and five explicitly scored components with no separate results; the components must not be treated as five additional effect estimates. Baseline Table 2 prints Group A N = 42, M = 11.46, S.D. = 7.12 and Group B N = 42, M = 12.86, S.D. = 8.23; t = 1.04; Sig. = 0.35, with no statistical significance at a 0.01 level. This baseline balance comparison is not coded as an AI effect. Arm-means/SDs/Ns availability flags use the Ns explicitly available in baseline Table 2; posttest-specific Ns and complete-pair counts remain unknown. No diversity, similarity, or delayed-retention outcome is reported. Lesson-plan appropriateness ratings and rubric-validation/reliability statistics are instrument checks, not student-output outcomes. No participant reuse, preregistration, data URL, or code URL is stated. Sig. = 0.00* is retained as printed and is not interpreted as a probability of exactly zero. No effect size was computed.
